#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR adds an accessor field for `service_health.go` (the one answering to LB HCs for eTP:Local) to the `healthz` state computed in `proxier_health.go`. It will then return a HTTP 200 is the service has a ready endpoint on the node AND if `healthz` is true.

We've found recently that the node handlers are feature gated, if we want to use this handlers we should remove the feature gate check on the Node informer https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111344#discussion_r936833738


https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d96af5f2761c23eddde206aee7b7147a9692b737/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go#L753-L766

> We've found recently that the node handlers are feature gated, if we want to use this handlers we should remove the feature gate check on the Node informer [#111344 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111344#discussion_r936833738)

Hmm, I would have imagined the node handler to be feature gated because `TopologyAwareHints` is, not because the node handler specifically is? If the latter is true, what does that even mean for the node handler to be feature gated - it's not a feature in itself, but more like a means to implementing a feature - like `TopologyAwareHints`.  

In any case: we could also just dial the Kubelet's healthz port on `localhost`, that should be equivalent to listing / watching the node object and inspecting if its `NodeReady` condition is `ConditionTrue`. The problem would be trying to work out the taints the node object has. But I would say the taint we currently look at (`ToBeDeletedByClusterAutoscaler`) is just pre-mature optimization for a node which will be deleted or go `NotReady` in the future. That taint doesn't mean anything _right now_, and if it really is going to be deleted in the near future, then we could just start flagging the node as "not serviceable for LB traffic" when that happens.  PR #105946 didn't really go a very good job at mentioning why we do this to begin with:

> Prior to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/90823, these nodes would get removed from the LoadBalancer backend once they were marked as Unschedulable. Now that Unschedulable nodes are tolerated by the node predicate, these nodes will only get removed when the nodes have been deleted. If multiple such nodes are being deleted, the list of nodes passed to cloud-provider code via UpdateLoadBalancer() will be stale, causing a few failed updates before the backends stabilize.

I was away for a bit but I spent all afternoon thinking about this topic and I am less confident than ever :)

An even more revised drawing (now v3):
![Node_LB_states_v3](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5595220/191383372-57cdc1f6-4be0-4f43-abcf-7bf60a8d2588.png)

A few things of note:

### 1) How to handle `deletionTimestamp` being set

a) We could exclude being-deleted nodes as a predicate (e.g. `notBeingDeletedPredicate`).  This is simple to do here, and well-behaved clusters already drained the node anyway (with `unschedulable`).  We might miss out on some extra draining time while being deleted, but that seems pretty minor (I don't think cluster-autoscaler uses finalizers).

b) Or we could NOT exclude them (but comment in code why not), and make the on-node HC fail while being deleted.  This gives us extra time to drain LB traffic, but well-behaved clusters already drained the node anyway (with `unschedulable`).

I think (a) is simpler and more obvious.

### How to handle the `ToBeDeletedByClusterAutoScaler` taint

See https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/issues/5201 for more context

a) We could exclude tained nodes (as we do today).  The way cluster-autoscaler seems to work means that down-scaled nodes would get `unschedulable` and `ToBeDeletedByClusterAutoScaler` set at the same time, and thus get no LB drain time (as we do today).

b) We could NOT exclude them (but comment in code why not) and maybe make the on-node HC fail.  I think this will break autoscalers who try to delete the underlying VM before the k8s node.  Perhaps we should use finalizers (clear it when all LBs have been updated), which would add weight to (1a) above.

I think we're foirced to do (a) for now, but I find it clumsy, and hope I am just mis-reading.

### How to handle `unschedulable` being true

We already do not handle this in the controller.

a) We could ignore it (as we do today).  Given that `unschedulable` often means a node is going away "soon", this would let such nodes handle new connections right up until it is deleted, which cause abrupt errors.

b) We could make all LB->Node HCs fail when `unschedulable` is set.  This would drain LB traffic on some clouds (no new connections, retain existing ones), which makes sense if you consider that `unschedulable` often means a node is going away "soon".   For `eTP: Local` services, this would mean any endpoints on that node are no longer available to serve, even during draining.  If you have a one-replica service and start draining the node that lone pod is on, the service will be unavailable until a new pod is started elsewhere.

c) We could make `eTP: Cluster` LB->Node HCs fail when `unschedulable` is set, while `eTP: Local` would pass.  This would drain "at-large" LB traffic on some clouds (no new connections, retain existing ones), which makes sense if you consider that `unschedulable` often means a node is going away "soon", but would let `eTP: Local` services continue to serve.  Presumable such pods would be gracefully terminated and restarted elsewhere.

I think (c) makes sense, but it a bit more subtle than we discussed before.

What do you think?

issue_context.title: Kube-proxy does not validate `healthz` state when answering to HC for eTP:Local
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

KEP https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3837 outlined the fact that Kube-proxy today doesn't perform any validation of its `healthz` state when answering to load balancer HCs for eTP:Local services.

This is a potential problem, because if Kube-proxy is unhealthy then it might also not be writing the rules needed to forward traffic to the endpoint on the node. This means that it might indicate to a load balancer that it should forward traffic to the node, simply because the endpoint is scheduled there



### What did you expect to happen?

Kube-proxy should perform the same validation it currently does for eTP:Local services (i.e: validate that the service has an endpoint scheduled and ready on the node) but AND it with its `healthz` state. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a service of `type: LoadBalancer` + `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`
2. Trigger an issue with Kube-proxy which causes it to fail when writing its rules on the node 
3. Spin up a pod for this service
4. Validate that Kube-proxy continues to indicate to the load balancer that it should send the node traffic, even though it hasn't been able to write the rules required as a consequence of 3. due to 2. 

### Anything else we need to know?
